Petrelintide (ZP8396): Amylin Analog for Obesity & Type 2 Diabetes — Research Dossier

Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

Petrelintide is a long-acting amylin analog peptide in Phase 3 development for obesity and type 2 diabetes, co-developed by Zealand Pharma with Roche and Genentech. With two completed Phase 2 trials — one in non-diabetic obesity (ZUPREME-1, March 2026) and one in obesity plus type 2 diabetes (ZUPREME-2, October 2026) — petrelintide has one of the most robust early-stage datasets of any amylin analog in the pipeline.

What is Petrelintide?

Petrelintide (investigational code ZP8396) is a synthetic once-weekly amylin analog — a peptide designed to mimic amylin, a hormone naturally co-secreted with insulin by pancreatic beta cells. Amylin signals fullness (satiety) through specific brain circuits, particularly the area postrema in the brainstem, and also suppresses post-meal glucagon secretion and slows gastric emptying. These effects are distinct from GLP-1 receptor signaling, making amylin analogs a mechanistically separate approach to appetite suppression and weight loss.

Earlier amylin analogs — most notably pramlintide (Symlin, FDA-approved 2005) — required two to three injections daily, limiting practical use for obesity. Petrelintide is engineered for once-weekly subcutaneous injection by modifying the molecule's half-life, making it compatible with modern weekly-dosing preferences.

The compound is developed under a partnership between Zealand Pharma (Denmark), which discovered and engineered the molecule, and Roche/Genentech (Switzerland/US), which licensed it in 2025 and is co-funding Phase 3 development.

Mechanism of Action

Petrelintide acts on the amylin receptor complex, a heterodimer of the calcitonin receptor (CTR) with a receptor activity-modifying protein (RAMP1, RAMP2, or RAMP3). This receptor complex is expressed in the brainstem area postrema — a region outside the blood-brain barrier that is exposed to circulating hormones and relays satiety signals to the hypothalamus.

Key downstream effects of amylin receptor activation include:

  • Satiety signaling: Reduces meal size and caloric intake through brainstem and hypothalamic circuits distinct from GLP-1 pathways
  • Glucagon suppression: Reduces post-meal glucagon secretion, limiting hepatic glucose output
  • Gastric emptying: Slows the rate of food leaving the stomach, prolonging satiety
  • Adipose modulation: May influence adipocyte function and fat mobilization (mechanism under investigation)

Because amylin and GLP-1 act via separate receptor systems and separate neural circuits, amylin analogs can in principle be combined with GLP-1 drugs for additive weight loss — a key rationale for the petrelintide + CT-388 combination trial planned by Roche.

Key Research Findings

Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 (Non-Diabetic Obesity)

Announced: March 5, 2026 (Roche/Genentech press release)

  • N=493 adults with overweight or obesity without type 2 diabetes (US)
  • Up to 10.7% mean weight loss at week 42 vs. 1.7% on placebo
  • Tolerability: side effects similar to placebo; nausea substantially lower than in Phase 1b; zero GI-related discontinuations at the maximally effective dose
  • Discontinuation rate: 4.8% on petrelintide vs. 4.9% on placebo — essentially identical
  • No unexpected safety signals identified
  • Full data (including 9-week safety follow-up) to inform Phase 3 design

Phase 2 ZUPREME-2 (Obesity + Type 2 Diabetes)

Announced: October 7, 2026 (Zealand Pharma company announcement #54/2026)

  • N=220 US adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes
  • Primary endpoint: body weight change at week 28
  • Up to 9.2% mean weight loss from baseline (range across arms: 7.4–9.2%) vs. 2.0% placebo
  • HbA1c reduction: placebo-adjusted reduction of 0.61–0.88% — demonstrating glycemic benefit
  • GI discontinuation: 1.9% petrelintide vs. 1.7% placebo — still near-indistinguishable from placebo
  • No unexpected safety signals
  • Full data to be presented at a scientific conference (Q4 2026 or Q1 2027)

Phase 3 Program: ZUPREME-3, -4, -5

Zealand Pharma and Roche have initiated the Phase 3 ZUPREME program targeting approximately 7,000 participants across three trials covering obesity (with and without T2DM) and potentially MASH. A Phase 2 combination trial of petrelintide plus Roche's enicepatide (CT-388 — a GLP-1/GIP dual agonist) is planned for initiation in H2 2026, targeting synergistic weight loss by engaging GLP-1, GIP, and amylin receptors simultaneously.

Dosing in Research

Specific dosing details for petrelintide are not yet fully published. Key available information:

  • Route: Subcutaneous injection
  • Frequency: Once weekly
  • Dose ranges: Multiple doses tested in both Phase 2 trials; the exact dose levels and individual arm results will be disclosed in peer-reviewed publications (expected Q4 2026 / Q1 2027 at scientific conference)
  • Important note: This compound is investigational and not available outside of clinical trials. Research dosing information is published for scientific context only — this does not constitute dosing guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How does petrelintide compare to eloralintide — both are amylin analogs for obesity?

Petrelintide (ZP8396, Zealand/Roche) and eloralintide (LY3841136, Eli Lilly) are both once-weekly selective amylin receptor agonists — the two most advanced amylin-only drugs in the pipeline. Petrelintide has completed two Phase 2 trials (ZUPREME-1 and ZUPREME-2) with Phase 3 now initiated. Eloralintide completed one Phase 2 (Lancet 2025, up to 20.1% at 48 weeks) with Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN launching in 2026. Eloralintide's Phase 2 weight loss appears numerically higher (20.1% vs. 10.7%), but the trials differ in duration, population, and dose levels — direct comparison is not valid. Petrelintide is distinguished by an exceptionally clean tolerability profile nearly indistinguishable from placebo for GI discontinuations. No head-to-head trial has been announced.

Q: Why is petrelintide being combined with enicepatide (CT-388)?

Enicepatide (CT-388) is Roche's GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, targeting the same receptors as tirzepatide but developed by Roche. A petrelintide + CT-388 combination would simultaneously engage GLP-1, GIP, and amylin receptors — three distinct satiety pathways. The scientific rationale: each pathway drives satiety via separate neural and hormonal circuits, potentially producing additive or synergistic weight loss beyond any dual-agonist. This mirrors Eli Lilly's EloraTZP strategy (eloralintide + tirzepatide). If the combination achieves 25–35% weight loss, it could define the next generation of obesity pharmacotherapy. The Phase 2 trial was planned for H2 2026 initiation.

Q: What is petrelintide's status in type 2 diabetes?

ZUPREME-2 specifically enrolled adults with obesity and T2DM, showing up to 9.2% weight loss at 28 weeks and HbA1c reductions of 0.61–0.88% vs. placebo. The glycemic benefit is consistent with amylin's known role in suppressing post-meal glucagon and slowing gastric emptying. The Phase 3 ZUPREME program (targeting ~7,000 participants) likely includes a T2DM + obesity registrational arm. Petrelintide is not approved for diabetes or obesity as of November 2026.

Research Limitations

  • Both ZUPREME-1 and ZUPREME-2 are Phase 2 trials — not yet sufficient for regulatory approval; Phase 3 data is needed
  • ZUPREME-2 topline results are company-reported; full data have not been peer-reviewed (expected Q4 2026 / Q1 2027)
  • 10.7% weight loss at 42 weeks is lower than the highest numbers seen with GLP-1/GIP dual agonists (tirzepatide: ~22% at 72 weeks), though head-to-head and longer follow-up have not been completed
  • Long-term safety data beyond 42–48 weeks is not yet available
  • No cardiovascular outcomes data
  • Combination trial with enicepatide is still in planning/early initiation stage
